title: Adding & Subtracting Integers
html:
An integer is any whole number, positive, negative, or zero. Adding and subtracting integers is all about direction on the number line.

Types of numbers — quick reference
Natural numbers: 1, 2, 3, … (counting numbers)
Whole numbers: 0, 1, 2, 3, … (natural + zero)
Integers: …, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, … (whole + negatives)
Rational numbers: any number writable as a fraction (includes integers, fractions, terminating/repeating decimals)
Key rules
Add positive → move RIGHT on the number line
Add negative → move LEFT on the number line
Subtract → flip the sign and add: a − b = a + (−b)

Tug-o-war method: same signs add, different signs subtract (keep the sign of the bigger absolute value)
Money analogy: positive = money in your pocket, negative = debt
6 Tips & Tricks for integer addition & subtraction
1. Flipping a subtraction: a − b = a + (−b). Subtraction is just adding a negative.
2. Subtracting vs. adding a negative: 5 − 3 and 5 + (−3) give the same result — they mean the same thing!
3. Subtracting a negative: a − (−b) = a + b. Two negatives flip to a positive. (−)(−) = +
4. Adding two negatives: (−a) + (−b) = −(a + b). Same signs → add & keep the negative.
5. Tug-o-war: different signs? The bigger absolute value wins; subtract the smaller and keep that sign.
6. Think money: positive = money you have, negative = debt. −3 + 8 means you owe $3 but have $8 → $5 ahead.

Worked examples

Example 1 — −2 + 5
Start at −2, move right 5 spaces −2 + 5 = 3
Example 2 — −4 + (−7)
Same signs → add: 4 + 7 = 11, keep negative −4 + (−7) = −11
Example 3 — 3 − (−6)
Flip: 3 − (−6) = 3 + 6 = 9
Number Line: −3 + 5 = 2
Number Line: −4 + (−3) = −7  (negative + negative)

There’s no single right technique — pick what works for you on each problem.

title: Multiplying & Dividing Integers
html:
The key rule for multiplying and dividing integers is all about the signs. Let’s discover why by looking at a pattern.

Discover the pattern — why does positive × negative = negative?
Watch what happens as the second factor decreases by 1:
3 ×  2 =  6decreasing by 3 each time ↓
3 ×  1 =  3
3 ×  0 =  0
3 × (−1) = −3← keeps decreasing by 3
3 × (−2) = −6← pattern forces a negative
Notice the pattern → positive × negative = negative.
Now extend the same logic to negative × negative: if 3 × (−2) = −6, then (−3) × (−2) must flip the sign again → negative × negative = positive.
Sign rules
Same signs → positive answer
   (+)(+) = +    (−)(−) = +

Different signs → negative answer
   (+)(−) = −    (−)(+) = −

The same rules apply to division.

Worked examples

Example 1
(−4) × (−5) = +20 ← same signs = positive
Example 2
3 × (−7) = −21 ← different signs = negative
Example 3
(−18) ÷ (−3) = +6 ← same signs = positive

title: Order of Operations
html:
A numerical expression is a combination of numbers and operations. To evaluate it means to find its value. We always follow PEMDAS.

PEMDAS — Order of Operations
P — Parentheses (innermost first)
E — Exponents
M/D — Multiply & Divide (left to right)
A/S — Add & Subtract (left to right)

Memory trick: “Please Excuse My Dear Aunt Sally”

Operation vocabulary: Adding → sum  •  Subtracting → difference  •  Multiplying → product  •  Dividing → quotient

Worked examples

Example 1 — Evaluate: 3 + 4 × 2
Multiply first: 4 × 2 = 8 Then add: 3 + 8 = 11
Example 2 — Evaluate: (3 + 4) × 2
Parentheses first: 3 + 4 = 7 Then multiply: 7 × 2 = 14
Example 3 — Evaluate: 2² + 3 × (5 − 2)
P: (5 − 2) = 3 → 2² + 3 × 3 E: 2² = 4 → 4 + 3 × 3 M: 3 × 3 = 9 → 4 + 9 = 13

title: Introduction to Fractions
html:
A fraction represents part of a whole — like slicing a pizza into equal pieces: the denominator is how many slices, the numerator is how many you take. The numerator (top) tells how many parts you have. The denominator (bottom) tells how many equal parts the whole is split into.

Three forms of a negative fraction (all equivalent)
−ab  =  a−b  =  −ab

The first form (−ab) is preferred.
Example 1
34 means: 3 out of 4 equal parts
Example 2 — Equivalent fractions
12 = 24 = 36 = 48 (all the same value)
Example 3 — Negative fraction
−34 = 3−4 = −34 ← all equivalent; use −34
Fraction Model: 3/4 shaded
Number Line: fractions between 0 and 2

title: Simplifying Fractions
html:
To simplify a fraction, divide both the numerator and denominator by their GCF (Greatest Common Factor). The value of the fraction does not change — you just write it in a simpler form.

GCF Method
Step 1 — Find the GCF of numerator and denominator
Step 2 — Divide both by the GCF
Step 3 — Check: can it simplify further?
Example 1 — Simplify 812
GCF(8,12) = 4 8 ÷ 4 = 2,  12 ÷ 4 = 3 = 23
Example 2 — Simplify 1525
GCF(15,25) = 5 → 15/25 = 35
Example 3 — Simplify 1824
GCF(18,24) = 6 → 18/24 = 34
Alternatively: factor & cancel
You can also factor the numerator and denominator, then cancel common factors — same result as using the GCF.
Example: 1218 → 2 × 63 × 6 → 23  (the 6s cancel)

title: Adding & Subtracting Fractions
html:
Key insight
You can only add parts that are the same size. That’s why the denominators must match — the denominator tells you the size of each piece. You can’t add thirds to quarters until they’re the same piece size.

Same denominator: add or subtract the numerators only; keep the denominator. Different denominators: find the LCD (Least Common Denominator), convert each fraction to an equivalent fraction with that denominator, then add or subtract. Always simplify the answer.

Example 1 — Same denominator: 38 + 18
Same denominator → add numerators: 3 + 1 = 4 = 48 = 12
Example 2 — Different denominators: 14 + 13
LCD of 4 and 3 = 12 14 = 312    13 = 412 312 + 412 = 712
Example 3 — Subtraction: 56 − 14
LCD of 6 and 4 = 12 56 = 1012    14 = 312 1012 − 312 = 712
Common Denominator: 1/4 + 1/3 → 3/12 + 4/12

title: Multiplying & Dividing Fractions
html:
Multiply: multiply numerators together, multiply denominators together, then simplify. Divide: use Keep-Change-Flip (KCF) — keep the first fraction, change ÷ to ×, flip the second fraction, then multiply.

Keep-Change-Flip (KCF)
ab ÷ cd  →  Keep ab  ×  Flip dc
Example 1 — Multiply: 23 × 34
Numerators: 2 × 3 = 6    Denominators: 3 × 4 = 12 = 612 = 12
Example 2 — Divide: 34 ÷ 12
KCF: 34 × 21 = 64 = 32
Example 3 — Divide: 25 ÷ 45
KCF: 25 × 54 = 1020 = 12
Area Model: 2/3 × 3/4 = 6/12 = 1/2

title: Introduction to Variables
html:
A variable is a symbol (usually x or y) that represents an unknown number. Mr. Behling’s rule: “A variable is your friend — just a number. Don’t let it freak you out.”

Whatever you can do to a number, you can do to a variable. Add it, subtract it, multiply it, divide it — same rules, just with a letter standing in for the number.

Key ideas about variables
Multiplication shortcut: 2x means “2 times x” — no × symbol needed
Invisible coefficient: x = 1·x and −x = −1·x
Operations with variables look like: x+5, x−3, 4x, x/2
Example 1
x means “some unknown number” If x = 5, then x + 3 = 5 + 3 = 8
Example 2 — Invisible coefficient
x = 1x    −x = −1x
Example 3 — Reading expressions
4x = 4 times x    x/2 = x divided by 2

title: Adding & Subtracting Variables (Like Terms)
html:
Like terms have the same variable with the same exponent (or are both constants). You can only combine like terms — you cannot combine unlike terms.

The apple analogy
3 apples + 1 apple = 4 apples
3a + 1a = 4a    (same idea!)

3 apples + 1 banana ≠ 4 anything → cannot combine unlike terms
Example 1
3x + 5x = 8x ← like terms, add coefficients
Example 2
7y − 3y + 2y = 6y
Example 3 — Unlike terms
3x + 5 → cannot simplify (x-term and constant are unlike)

title: Multiplying Variables (Exponents)
html:
When you multiply the same variable repeatedly, use exponents as a shortcut. Mathematicians are lazy — we use shortcuts!

Common mistake — adding vs. multiplying
3x + 3x = 6x  (add coefficients — same idea as 3 apples + 3 apples = 6 apples)
3x · 3x = 9x²  (multiply coefficients AND add exponents)
Don’t mix them up! Adding keeps the same exponent; multiplying changes it.
Exponent shortcut for multiplying
x · x = x²    x · x · x = x³

When multiplying powers with the same base: ADD the exponents
x² · x³ = x&sup5;    x&sup4; · x = x&sup5;

Multiply coefficients separately: (2x³)(4x²) = 8x&sup5;
Example 1
x² · x³ = x(2+3) = x&sup5;
Example 2
(3x²)(5x³) = 15x&sup5; ← multiply coefficients, add exponents
Example 3
(2x³)(4x²) = 8x&sup5;
Reading aloud & order doesn’t matter
Reading exponents: x² = “x squared” or “x to the second power”  •  x³ = “x cubed”  •  x&sup4; = “x to the fourth”
Commutativity: Multiplication can be done in any order — (3x²)(5x³) = (5x³)(3x²) = 15x&sup5;. Pick the order that feels easiest!

title: The Language of Algebra
html:
Algebra has its own vocabulary. Understanding the parts of an expression is like understanding the parts of a sentence.

Anatomy of an Expression: 3x² + 2x − 9
Equation vs. Expression: 3x + 5 = 11
Key vocabulary
Term: a number, a variable, or a number times a variable (e.g., 3x, −5, x²)
Coefficient: the number in front of the variable (e.g., in 3x, the coefficient is 3)
Constant: a term with no variable (just a number, e.g., 7)
Algebraic expression: one or more terms combined with + or − (no equal sign)
Equation: has an equal sign.  Expression: no equal sign.
Example 1 — Identify parts of 3x + 5
Terms: 3x and 5 Coefficient of x: 3 Constant: 5
Example 2 — Expression or Equation?
2x + 7 → Expression (no = sign) 2x + 7 = 11 → Equation (has = sign)
Example 3 — Identify: −4x² + 2x − 9
3 terms. Coefficients: −4 and 2. Constant: −9
Invisible 1 coefficient
When you see just “x” with no number in front, the coefficient is 1 (it’s invisible). So x = 1x, −x = −1x, and x² = 1x². Never forget the hidden 1!

title: Simplifying Expressions
html:
To simplify an expression: (1) Distribute to remove parentheses, (2) Combine like terms. Say it out loud when distributing!

Distributive Property: 3(x + 4)
Distributive Property
a(b + c) = ab + ac

Draw arcs from the outside term to each inside term. Say it out loud!

Watch the negative! Circle the negative sign before parentheses.
−(x + 3) = −1(x + 3) = −x − 3
Example 1 — Simplify: 3(x + 4) − 2x
Distribute: 3x + 12 − 2x Combine like terms: x + 12
Example 2 — Simplify: −(x + 3) + 5x
Circle the negative: −1(x + 3) + 5x Distribute: −x − 3 + 5x Combine: 4x − 3
Example 3 — Simplify: 2(3x − 1) + 4
Distribute: 6x − 2 + 4 Combine constants: 6x + 2
Standard ordering rule
Write your final answer from highest to lowest exponent, with the constant last. Example: 3x² + 2x − 5. This is called standard form for a polynomial.

title: Evaluating Expressions
html:
To evaluate an expression, replace the variable with the given number (use parentheses!), then use PEMDAS. Remember: “A variable is just a number. Don’t let it freak you out.”

Process
Step 1 — Substitute (replace x with the given number, put in parentheses)
Step 2 — Use PEMDAS to evaluate
Example 1 — Evaluate 3x − 5 when x = 4
3(4) − 5 = 12 − 5 = 7
Example 2 — Evaluate 3x − 5 when x = −2
3(−2) − 5 = −6 − 5 = −11
Example 3 — Evaluate 3x − 5 when x = 0
3(0) − 5 = 0 − 5 = −5

title: Solving Basic Equations
html:
Before you begin — expected prior knowledge
This topic builds on vocabulary from Units 3 & 4. Make sure you know:
Term — a number, variable, or their product (e.g., 3x, −5, x²)
Coefficient — the number in front of the variable
Constant — a term with no variable
Algebraic expression — terms combined with + or −, no equal sign
Equation — has an equal sign; two expressions set equal

Connect to prior knowledge: An equation is a statement that two algebraic expressions are equal — think of it like a scale. Both sides are balanced. Whatever you do to one side you must do to the other. Always. A variable is just a number we don't know yet — don't let it freak you out!

Key concept — solution
A solution to an equation is a number that, when you plug it in for x, makes the equation true. That's the magic number we're solving for.

5 key principles for organizing your work

  1. Work vertically — top down. Do not work left to right. Do not erase.
  2. Line up your equal signs. Draw a vertical line through the equal sign to stay organized.
  3. Whatever you do to one side, you do to the other. Always. This keeps the equation balanced.
  4. Keep going until x is by itself. Circle it. That's the goal.
  5. Write “Check” and substitute your answer back in. Use ✓ if it works, ✗ if it doesn't.

The “Undo” table — your most important tool

Ask: what is happening to x? List it top-to-bottom following PEMDAS. Then undo in reverse order bottom-to-top.

↓ fill in top to bottomundo bottom to top ↑
What's happening to xHow to undo it
Adding a number  (x + 5)→Subtract from both sides
Subtracting a number  (x − 5)→Add to both sides
Multiplying by a number  (3x)→Divide both sides by that number
Dividing by a number  (x ÷ 4)→Multiply both sides by that number
Gotcha — the invisible coefficient
When you see −x, there is a −1 right there — it's invisible. So −x is really −1·x. Watch your signs!

Worked example 1 — basic two-step: solve 3x − 7 = 14

Worked example — undo table + check
↓ x is ×3, then −7undo: +7 first, then ÷3 ↑
What's happening to xUndo
Multiply by 3→Divide both sides by 3
Subtract 7→Add 7 to both sides (do this FIRST — reverse!)
3x − 7  =  14       +7     +7 ← add 7 first (bottom of undo table)      3x  =  21       ÷3     ÷3       x  =  7  ✓ Check: 3(7) − 7 = 21 − 7 = 14 ✓

Worked example 2 — fraction result: solve 2x + 5 = 12

Worked example — fraction answer is fine!
2x + 5  =  12       −5     −5      2x  =  7       ÷2     ÷2       x  =  7/2  ✓ ← a fraction is just a number. Don't panic! Check: 2(7/2) + 5 = 7 + 5 = 12 ✓

Worked example 3 — the gotcha: solve 6 − x = 13

Worked example — invisible −1! Your radar should be up.
6 − x  =  13 ← −x means −1·x. The coefficient is −1!   −6        −6      −x  =  7  ÷(−1)   ÷(−1)       x  =  −7  ✓ Check: 6 − (−7) = 6 + 7 = 13 ✓
Joke: “Hey, you knew x was 7 the whole time. Why didn't you say something?”

title: Solving Equations with Fractions
html:
Good news and bad news. Bad news: fractions show up in equations. Ugghh!!! Good news: we can use the exact same technique from 5.1. Same undo table — no new tools needed.

Case 1 — x divided by a number: solve x/4 + 3 = 8

Worked example — Case 1
x/4 + 3  =  8 ← x is ÷4, then +3. Undo: −3 first, then ×4        −3     −3      x/4  =  5        ×4     ×4        x  =  20  ✓ Check: 20/4 + 3 = 5 + 3 = 8 ✓

Case 2 — x multiplied by a fraction: solve (2/3)x = 10

Worked example — Case 2 — multiply by the reciprocal
(2/3)x  =  10 ← x is ×(2/3). Undo: multiply by the reciprocal 3/2 (3/2)·(2/3)x  =  10·(3/2) ← the 2s and 3s cancel         x  =  15  ✓ Check: (2/3)(15) = 10 ✓

Case 3 — compound fraction: solve (3x + 1)/4 = 5

Worked example — Case 3 — watch the implicit parentheses!
(3x + 1)/4  =  5 ← think: (3x + 1) ÷ 4 = 5. Undo ÷4 first              ×4     ×4        3x + 1  =  20              −1     −1             3x  =  19              ÷3     ÷3              x  =  19/3  ✓ Check: (3(19/3)+1)/4 = 20/4 = 5 ✓
Sign errors in numerators
When you see (6 − 3x)/5, think (6 − 3x) ÷ 5. The −3 stays with x. Say it out loud: “negative three times x.”
Joke: 4 out of 3 people struggle with fractions.

title: Solving More Complex Equations
html:
What if an equation has parentheses, multiple terms on each side, or x on both sides? Double underline that. We have a process — and we already know most of it.

Process for solving equations (4 steps)
Step 1 — Simplify each side completely:
  • Distribute to remove parentheses — circle negative signs first
  • Combine like terms on each side
  • Strategy tip: Cover the right side with your hand and fully simplify the left first, then switch. One side at a time!

Step 2 — Get x on one side. Move the x term with the smaller coefficient — fewer negatives means fewer mistakes.

Step 3 — Undo using the table from 5.1

Step 4 — Check your solution
Negative sign before parentheses
When you see −(2x + 7), write a 1: −1(2x + 7). Circle that −1. It multiplies every term inside. Say it out loud as you go.

Worked example — solve: 2(x + 4) = 3x − 1

Worked example
2(x + 4)  =  3x − 1 2x + 8  =  3x − 1 ← distribute −2x           −2x ← move smaller coefficient (2 < 3) 8  =  x − 1 +1              +1 9  =  x  ✓ Check: 2(9+4) = 26; 3(9)−1 = 26 ✓

Worked example 2 — x on both sides: solve 5x − 3 = 2x + 9

Worked example — x on both sides
5x − 3  =  2x + 9 ← x on both sides; move the smaller (2x) −2x           −2x 3x − 3  =  9       +3     +3       3x  =  12       ÷3     ÷3        x  =  4  ✓ Check: 5(4)−3=17; 2(4)+9=17 ✓

Worked example 3 — negative distribution: solve 4 − 3(x + 2) = −5

Worked example — circle the negative before distributing!
4 − 3(x + 2)  =  −5 4 − 3x − 6  =  −5 ← circle −3; distribute to BOTH terms −3x − 2  =  −5 ← combine 4 and −6        +2      +2       −3x  =  −3  ÷(−3)   ÷(−3)         x  =  1  ✓ Check: 4−3(1+2)=4−9=−5 ✓
Joke: “Dear Algebra, please stop asking me to find your x. She's not coming back and don't ask y.”

title: Special Case Equations
html:
Important: we solve equations. We simplify and evaluate algebraic expressions. An equation has an equal sign. An expression does not. You cannot solve an expression.

Common sense first — try numbers in: x + 1 = x + 2
x = 7:  7+1=8  vs  7+2=9  →  8≠9. No. x = 0:  0+1=1  vs  0+2=2  →  1≠2. No. How could any number +1 equal the same number +2? It just can't.
The rule — when x disappears in Step 2
FALSE statement (like 3 = 7) → No Solution
Would you rather have $1 or $2? Not equal. No value of x works.

TRUE statement (like 6 = 6) → All Real Numbers
Every number makes the equation true.

No Solution — solve: 2x + 3 = 2x + 9

Worked example
2x + 3  =  2x + 9 −2x           −2x 3  =  9  ← FALSE → No Solution

All Real Numbers — solve: 12x − 3(x − 2) = 9x + 6

Worked example
12x − 3(x − 2)  =  9x + 6 9x + 6  =  9x + 6 ← distribute, combine −9x         −9x 6  =  6  ← TRUE → All Real Numbers Check: pick any number — they all work.
Joke: “Just another thing I hate about algebra… when the solution is ‘no solution’. Ugghh!!!”

title: Writing & Graphing Inequalities
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: You already know what an equation looks like: two expressions set equal. An inequality is similar, but instead of saying two sides are equal, it says one side is greater than, less than, or “at least” or “at most” the other. Don't let it freak you out — it's just a bigger version of the same idea.

Key concept — inequality symbols
<  less than
>  greater than
≤  less than or equal to (closed dot on graph)
≥  greater than or equal to (closed dot on graph)

Alligator trick: The alligator always eats the bigger number — its mouth opens toward the larger side.
Read backwards: When x is on the right (e.g., 4 < x), flip and read “x is greater than 4.” That way you're always saying what x is.

More than one symbol can be true: For the statement 3 __ 7, the blanks <, ≤, and ≠ all make true statements! Inequalities describe a relationship, not just a single comparison.

Graphing inequalities on a number line

Chart for graphing inequalities
Strict (< or >): Open circle — the endpoint is NOT included
Non-strict (≤ or ≥): Closed (filled) circle — the endpoint IS included
Greater than: arrow points right  →
Less than: arrow points left  ←

Worked examples

Example 1 — graph x > 3
x > 3 → open circle at 3, arrow pointing right “x is greater than 3”
Example 2 — graph x ≤ −1
x ≤ −1 → closed circle at −1, arrow pointing left “x is less than or equal to negative one”
Example 3 — write inequality from graph (open circle at 2, arrow right)
Open circle = strict. Arrow right = greater than. → x > 2
Joke: How do you make seven even? Take away the “s”.

title: Solving Basic Inequalities
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: Solving an inequality is nearly identical to solving an equation. Same undo table, same steps — with one critical exception.

Warm-up — is a value a solution to an inequality?
Before solving, let's practice checking whether a specific x-value satisfies an inequality.

Example: Is x = 3 a solution to 2x − 1 > 4?
Substitute: 2(3) − 1 = 5. Is 5 > 4? Yes ✓ → x = 3 IS a solution.

Is x = 2 a solution to the same inequality?
Substitute: 2(2) − 1 = 3. Is 3 > 4? No ✗ → x = 2 is NOT a solution.
The ONE rule that’s different
When you multiply or divide both sides of an inequality by a negative number, you must flip the inequality sign.

Why? Think about it: 2 < 8 is true. Multiply both sides by −1: −2 < −8? No! −2 > −8. The relationship flipped.

Say it out loud every single time you divide or multiply by a negative: “flip the sign.”

Worked example 1 — solve and graph: 3x − 6 < 9

Worked example — positive coefficient (no flip)
3x − 6 < 9       +6    +6       3x < 15       ÷3    ÷3        x < 5  ✓ Graph: open circle at 5, arrow left

Worked example 2 — solve and graph: −4x ≥ 20

Worked example — NEGATIVE coefficient (FLIP!)
−4x ≥ 20 ÷(−4)  ÷(−4)  ← FLIP THE SIGN!      x ≤ −5  ✓ Graph: closed circle at −5, arrow left

Worked example 3 — solve and graph: x/(−2) ≤ 3

Worked example — dividing by negative (FLIP!)
x/(−2) ≤ 3 ×(−2)  ×(−2)  ← FLIP!        x ≥ −6  ✓ Graph: closed circle at −6, arrow right
When do you flip?
Only when you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number. Adding or subtracting a negative does NOT require a flip.
Joke: What is a butterfly's favorite subject? Mothematics.

title: Solving More Complex Inequalities
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: Now we bring in parentheses, like terms, and variables on both sides — just like Topic 5.3 for equations. The same 4-step process applies, with the added flip rule from 6.2.

Process for solving inequalities (4 steps)
Step 1 — Simplify each side: Distribute & combine like terms
Step 2 — Get x on one side: Move the smaller coefficient
Step 3 — Undo: Use the undo steps (and flip if you multiply/divide by negative!)
Step 4 — Graph the solution on a number line

Worked example 1 — solve: 2(x + 3) ≤ 4x − 2

Worked example
2(x + 3) ≤ 4x − 2 2x + 6 ≤ 4x − 2 ← distribute −2x      −2x ← move smaller coeff 6 ≤ 2x − 2 +2         +2 8 ≤ 2x → x ≥ 4 ← read backwards Graph: closed circle at 4, arrow right

Worked example 2 — solve: −3(x − 2) > 12

Worked example — negative distribution, then divide by negative
−3(x − 2) > 12 −3x + 6 > 12 ← circle the −3! distribute         −6    −6      −3x > 6 ÷(−3)  ÷(−3)  ← FLIP!        x < −2  ✓

Worked example 3 — solve: 5x + 1 > 3x − 7

Worked example
5x + 1 > 3x − 7 −3x       −3x 2x + 1 > −7      −1    −1     2x > −8     ÷2   ÷2      x > −4  ✓

title: Special Case Inequalities
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: In Unit 5 we saw two special cases when solving equations: No Solution and All Real Numbers. The same thing can happen with inequalities!

Special case rules for inequalities
When x cancels out in Step 2:
FALSE statement (e.g., 3 > 7) → No Solution
TRUE statement (e.g., 5 < 9) → All Real Numbers

Same rule as equations — just check if the leftover statement is true or false.

Worked example 1 — No Solution: solve 3x + 5 > 3x + 8

Worked example
3x + 5 > 3x + 8 −3x       −3x 5 > 8 ← FALSE → No Solution No value of x makes 5 > 8 true.

Worked example 2 — All Real Numbers: solve 2x − 1 < 2x + 4

Worked example
2x − 1 < 2x + 4 −2x      −2x −1 < 4 ← TRUE → All Real Numbers Every number x makes this true.
Joke: Why is the equal sign so humble? Because she knows she's not greater than or less than anyone else.

title: Compound Inequalities
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: A compound inequality is two inequalities joined by and or or. Think about driving: you must go at least 45 mph but no more than 65 mph. That's a compound inequality: 45 ≤ speed ≤ 65.

Two types of compound inequalities
“And” (intersection): Both conditions must be true. Graph = overlap of both graphs.
  Example: x > −2 AND x ≤ 4 can be written compactly as −2 < x ≤ 4 — same meaning, just shorter.
  Tip: read the compact form from left to right: “−2 is less than x, and x is less than or equal to 4.”

“Or” (union): At least one condition is true. Graph = both graphs combined.
  Example: x < −3 OR x ≥ 1

The “In-Between” problem — solve: −2 ≤ 3x + 1 < 10

Key principle for “in-between” problems
Whatever you do to one side, you do to ALL THREE sides!
Worked example — in-between problem
−2 ≤ 3x + 1 < 10 −1       −1  −1 ← subtract 1 from all 3 parts −3 ≤ 3x < 9 ÷3    ÷3  ÷3 −1 ≤ x < 3  ✓ Graph: closed circle at −1, open circle at 3, shaded between

Worked example — “Or” compound: solve 2x + 1 < −5 OR 3x − 2 ≥ 7

Worked example — solve each separately
Left: 2x + 1 < −5 → 2x < −6 → x < −3 Right: 3x − 2 ≥ 7 → 3x ≥ 9 → x ≥ 3 Solution: x < −3 OR x ≥ 3

title: Relations & Functions
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: You have been working with x- and y-values all year. A relation is simply any pairing of x-values (inputs) with y-values (outputs). A function is a special kind of relation with one extra rule.

What is a Relation?
A relation is any set of ordered pairs (x, y). It can be shown as:
• A mapping diagram — bubbles on the left map to bubbles on the right
• A table — two columns, x and y
• A set of ordered pairs — e.g., {(1,2), (3,4)}
• A graph — points or curves on the coordinate plane
What is a Function?
A function is a relation where each x-value is paired with EXACTLY ONE y-value.

Think of it like a vending machine: each button (x) gives you exactly one item (y). If pressing button B3 sometimes gives chips and sometimes gives candy, it's not a function!

The one rule: No x-value can repeat with a different y-value.

Vertical Line Test (VLT)

Vertical Line Test
If you can draw a vertical line anywhere on a graph and it crosses the graph more than once, it is NOT a function.
If every vertical line crosses at most once → IS a function.
Vertical Line Test

Discrete vs. Continuous

Discrete vs. Continuous Graphs
Discrete: Individual, unconnected dots. The values are separate (e.g., number of students).
Continuous: A connected curve or line. The values flow without gaps (e.g., temperature over time).

Worked examples

Example 1 — Is {(1,3),(2,5),(3,3)} a function?
x-values: 1, 2, 3 — all different ✓ Each x pairs with exactly one y. → YES, it is a function.
Example 2 — Is {(2,4),(3,7),(2,9)} a function?
x = 2 appears twice (paired with 4 and 9). One x goes to TWO different y-values! → NO, NOT a function.
Example 3 — VLT on a circle vs. a line
Circle: a vertical line in the middle crosses at 2 points → NOT a function. A straight diagonal line: any vertical line crosses once → IS a function.
Joke: Math teachers have been putting the “fun” in functions since time t = 0.

title: Domain & Range
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: Now that we know what a relation is, we need vocabulary for describing all the inputs and outputs it uses.

Domain & Range
Domain = the set of all x-values (inputs). Domain comes before Range — just like X comes before Y in the alphabet!
Range = the set of all y-values (outputs).

Memory trick: “D comes before R, X comes before Y.”
Shadow Technique
Domain (x-values): Imagine a flashlight shining straight down onto the x-axis. The shadow shows which x-values are used.
Range (y-values): Imagine a flashlight shining sideways onto the y-axis. The shadow shows which y-values are used.
Shadow Technique — Domain & Range
• Domain = {1,3,5}  (flashlight straight down → x-shadow)    • Range = {2,3,4}  (flashlight sideways → y-shadow)

Other names for the coordinate plane

Names for the x-y plane
The coordinate plane has several names:
• Cartesian plane (named after mathematician René Descartes)
• xy-plane
• Coordinate plane

Worked examples

Example 1 — Table: find domain & range
x: 1, 3, 5, 7   |   y: 2, 6, 10, 14 Domain = {1, 3, 5, 7} Range = {2, 6, 10, 14}
Example 2 — Ordered pairs: {(2,5),(4,7),(-1,3)}
Domain = {-1, 2, 4} (all x-values, list in order) Range = {3, 5, 7} (all y-values, list in order)
Example 3 — Discrete graph with 4 points
Points: (0,1), (2,3), (4,5), (-2,1) Domain = {-2, 0, 2, 4} Range = {1, 3, 5} (don't list 1 twice!)
Joke: I love math puns. They are right in my domain.

title: Linear Functions
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: You have graphed lines before. Now we identify which functions are linear — meaning they form a straight line when graphed — and which are not.

What makes a function linear?
A linear function has a CONSTANT RATE OF CHANGE (the slope is always the same).

Three ways to identify:
• Graph: forms a straight line
• Table: y-values change by the same amount each step (constant differences)
• Ordered pairs: slope between any two points is constant

General form: y = mx + b (slope-intercept form, coming up in Unit 8!)
Non-linear clue
If the differences in y-values are NOT constant in a table, or if the graph is a curve, it is NOT linear.

Worked examples — tables

Example 1 — Linear table
x: 1, 2, 3, 4   |   y: 3, 5, 7, 9 Differences in y: 5-3=2, 7-5=2, 9-7=2 → constant! → LINEAR function ✓
Example 2 — Non-linear table
x: 1, 2, 3, 4   |   y: 1, 4, 9, 16 Differences in y: 3, 5, 7 → NOT constant! → NOT linear (this is y = x², a parabola)
Example 3 — Linear from equation
Is y = 2x + 1 linear? → YES (it's in y = mx + b form) Is y = x² + 3 linear? → NO (there is an exponent on x)
Exception — vertical lines
A vertical line (e.g., x = 3) is NOT a linear function — it fails the Vertical Line Test because one x-value maps to infinitely many y-values. Vertical lines have undefined slope and are not functions at all.

title: Function Notation
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: We have been writing functions as y = expression. Function notation is a new way to write the same thing, and it makes it crystal clear what the input and output are.

Reading f(x)
f(x) is read “f of x” — where f is the name of the function and x is the input.
f(x) replaces y. So y = 3x − 2 becomes f(x) = 3x − 2.

You can use other letters too: g(x), h(x), k(x).

f(x) does NOT mean f times x!
Forward vs. Backward Problems
Forward problems: Given an x-value, find f(x). Just substitute and simplify.
  Example: “Find f(4)” → plug in x = 4.

Backward problems: Given f(x) = some number, find x. Solve like an equation.
  Example: “If f(x) = 10, find x” → set expression = 10 and solve.

Worked examples

Forward: f(x) = 3x − 2
f(4) = 3(4) − 2 = 12 − 2 = 10 f(-1) = 3(-1) − 2 = -3 − 2 = -5 f(0) = 3(0) − 2 = 0 − 2 = -2
Backward: f(x) = 3x − 2, find x when f(x) = 10
3x − 2 = 10      +2   +2       3x = 12      ÷3  ÷3        x = 4 ✓
Joke: What did one algebra student say to another? Don't bother me. I have my own problems.

title: What is Slope?
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: You've graphed points on a coordinate plane. Slope describes how steep a line is — how much it rises or falls as you move from left to right.

Intuition first
If you had to describe a line to a friend over the phone, you'd say two things: where it starts and how steeply it tilts. Slope is the “tilt” number — positive means uphill left-to-right, negative means downhill, zero means flat.
Slope Formula
slope = rise / run = (y₂ − y₁) / (x₂ − x₁)

Positive slope: line goes up from left to right
Negative slope: line goes down from left to right
Zero slope: horizontal line (no rise)
Undefined slope: vertical line (no run — division by zero)
Slope Directions at a Glance

Worked example 1 — slope from two points (2, 3) and (6, 11)

Worked example
m = (y₂ − y₁) / (x₂ − x₁) m = (11 − 3) / (6 − 2) = 8/4 = 2 ✓

Worked example 2 — slope from (1, 5) and (4, −1)

Worked example — negative slope
Label: (x₁,y₁) = (1,5)   (x₂,y₂) = (4,−1) m = (y₂ − y₁) / (x₂ − x₁) = (−1 − 5) / (4 − 1) m = −6 / 3 = −2  ← negative: line goes down left-to-right

Worked example 3 — special slopes

Zero and undefined
(2, 4) and (7, 4): m = (4−4)/(7−2) = 0/5 = 0 → horizontal (3, 1) and (3, 9): m = (9−1)/(3−3) = 8/0 → undefined → vertical

Worked example 4 — slope from a table

Worked example — slope from a table
x:   0    1    2    3 y:   1    4    7    10 y-differences: 4−1=3   7−4=3   10−7=3 ← constant every step x-differences: all +1 m = (change in y) ÷ (change in x) = 3 ÷ 1 = 3 ✓
Joke: Why was the math book sad? Because it had too many problems.

title: Slope-Intercept Form
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: Once you know the slope, you can write a complete equation for a line using slope-intercept form.

Slope-Intercept Form
y = mx + b
m = slope    b = y-intercept (where the line crosses the y-axis)
How to graph y = mx + b (3 steps)
Step 1: Plot the y-intercept (0, b) on the y-axis
Step 2: Use slope (rise/run) to find the next point
Step 3: Draw a line through both points
Graph: y = 2x + 1 (m=2, b=1)

Worked example — graph y = 2x + 1

Worked example
m = 2, b = 1 Step 1: plot (0, 1) Step 2: slope 2/1 → go up 2, right 1 → plot (1, 3) Step 3: draw line through (0,1) and (1,3) ✓

Worked example — identify m and b from y = −(3/4)x + 5

Identify slope and y-intercept
m = −34 (slope is negative → line goes down) b = 5 (y-intercept is 5)
Finding the x-intercept
The x-intercept is where the line crosses the x-axis (y = 0).
From the equation: set y = 0 and solve for x.
From the graph: look for where the line meets the horizontal axis.

Worked example — x-intercept of y = 2x − 6

Finding the x-intercept
Set y = 0:   0 = 2x − 6 Add 6:      6 = 2x Divide by 2:   x = 3 → x-intercept is (3, 0) ✓
Joke: I told an algebra joke. No response. I guess x didn't care.

title: Writing Equations of Lines
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: You can write the equation of any line if you know enough information. The most useful tools are point-slope form and slope-intercept form.

Which form to use?
Point-slope form y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) → use when you have a point and the slope
Slope-intercept form y = mx + b → use when you have the slope and y-intercept
Both lead to the same final equation — choose whichever feels faster.
Given slope and a point
Use point-slope form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)
Plug in m, x₁, y₁ → simplify to slope-intercept form (y = mx + b)

Worked example 1 — slope = 3, through (2, 7)

Worked example — slope=3, point (2,7)
Plug into point-slope: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) y − 7 = 3(x − 2) ← m=3, x₁=2, y₁=7 y − 7 = 3x − 6 ← distribute y = 3x + 1 ✓
Given two points
Step 1: Find slope: m = (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁)
Step 2: Use point-slope form with one of the points
Step 3: Simplify to y = mx + b

Worked example 2 — through (1, 4) and (3, 10)

Worked example
m = (10−4)/(3−1) = 6/2 = 3 y − 4 = 3(x − 1) y − 4 = 3x − 3 y = 3x + 1 ✓

title: Standard Form & Special Lines
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: Standard form is another way to write linear equations. It's especially useful for finding intercepts quickly.

Standard Form
Ax + By = C where A, B, C are integers and A ≥ 0

Find x-intercept: set y = 0, solve for x
Find y-intercept: set x = 0, solve for y

Worked example — find intercepts of 3x + 2y = 12

Worked example
x-intercept: set y=0 → 3x = 12 → x = 4 → (4, 0) y-intercept: set x=0 → 2y = 12 → y = 6 → (0, 6)
Graph: 3x + 2y = 12
Special Lines
Horizontal line: y = k (slope = 0, passes through (0, k))
Vertical line: x = h (undefined slope, passes through (h, 0))
Special line examples
y = 4 → horizontal line, all points have y-coordinate 4 x = −3 → vertical line, all points have x-coordinate −3
Big picture — “backward” problems
Forward problem: given an equation → graph it.
Backward problem: given a graph or description → write the equation.
Writing equations (8.3) is the backward version of graphing (8.2). Both directions show up on every test.

title: Graphing Linear Inequalities
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: In Unit 6, you graphed inequalities on a number line. In Unit 8, you graphed linear equations as lines. Now put them together: a linear inequality is graphed as a boundary line plus a shaded region showing all points that make the inequality true.

Two Rules for Graphing Inequalities
Rule 1 — Boundary line:
• Dashed line for strict < or >  (boundary is NOT included)
• Solid line for ≤ or ≥  (boundary IS included — on the line counts!)

Rule 2 — Shading direction (after solving for y):
• y > … or y ≥ … → shade above the line
• y < … or y ≤ … → shade below the line
Mr. Behling's trick
After getting y by itself, look at the inequality sign: “>” points UP → shade ABOVE. “<” points DOWN → shade BELOW. Works every time!
Boundary Line: Dashed (< or >) vs. Solid (≤ or ≥)

5-Step process for graphing a linear inequality

  1. Solve the inequality for y (get y alone on the left)
  2. Graph the boundary line using slope-intercept form
  3. Draw dashed for < or >; draw solid for ≤ or ≥
  4. Shade above for y > or y ≥; shade below for y < or y ≤
  5. Check: plug (0, 0) into the original inequality — if true, you shaded the correct side

Worked example 1 — graph y > 2x − 1

Worked example — strict inequality (>)
Step 1: y is already isolated: y > 2x − 1 Step 2: boundary line y = 2x − 1   m = 2, b = −1 Step 3: > is strict → draw a dashed line Step 4: y > … → shade above the line Check: test (0, 0):   0 > 2(0) − 1 → 0 > −1 ✓   Correct side!

Worked example 2 — graph 2x + y ≤ 4

Worked example — first solve for y
Step 1: solve for y:   2x + y ≤ 4 → y ≤ −2x + 4 Step 2: boundary line y = −2x + 4   m = −2, b = 4 Step 3: ≤ → draw a solid line Step 4: y ≤ … → shade below the line Check: test (0, 0):   2(0) + 0 ≤ 4 → 0 ≤ 4 ✓   Correct side!
Mr. Behling says: If you can graph a line and solve an inequality, you can do this. It's just both at once!

title: What is a System of Equations?
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: You already know how to check if an ordered pair is a solution to a single equation. Now we level up — a system of equations requires the ordered pair to satisfy BOTH equations at the same time.

Real-world “systems”
You already use systems every day. Your digestive system is many organs working together as one unit. A city's transportation system is many routes that all connect. In math, a system of equations is two rules that must both be true at the same time — your job is to find the one point where that happens.
Key concept — system of equations
A system of equations is a group of linear equations that depend on each other and must be solved together.

We solve systems of 2 linear equations with 2 variables (x and y).

To solve = find the ordered pair (x, y) that makes BOTH equations true simultaneously.
Mr. Behling says: Don't let it freak you out — it's just two equations working together.

Checking if an ordered pair is a solution

Process for checking a solution
Step 1: Substitute the x and y values into Equation 1. Does it work?
Step 2: Substitute the same x and y values into Equation 2. Does it work?
Both must be true for it to be a solution to the system.

Worked example 1 — Is (2, 3) a solution?

Check (2, 3) in y = x + 1 and x + y = 5
Equation 1: y = x + 1 → 3 = 2 + 1 → 3 = 3 ✓ Equation 2: x + y = 5 → 2 + 3 = 5 → 5 = 5 ✓ Both true → Yes, (2, 3) IS a solution.

Worked example 2 — Is (−1, 4) a solution?

Check (−1, 4) in y = −3x + 1 and 2x + y = 2
Equation 1: y = −3x + 1 → 4 = −3(−1) + 1 → 4 = 3 + 1 → 4 = 4 ✓ Equation 2: 2x + y = 2 → 2(−1) + 4 = 2 → −2 + 4 = 2 → 2 = 2 ✓ Both true → Yes, (−1, 4) IS a solution.

title: Solving Systems by Graphing
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: Each equation in a system is a line. You already know how to graph lines using slope-intercept form. Now graph both lines and find where they intersect.

Key idea
The intersection point is the solution — it is the one point that satisfies BOTH equations at the same time.

Process for solving by graphing

  1. Graph both lines using slope-intercept form (y = mx + b)
  2. Identify the intersection point (where the lines cross)
  3. Write as ordered pair (x, y) — that is your answer
  4. Check: substitute back into both equations to verify

Three possibilities when graphing 2 lines

What can happen?
One solution: Lines cross at one point (different slopes) → intersection point is the answer

No solution: Lines are parallel — same slope, different y-intercept → they never meet

Infinite solutions: Lines are the same line (coincident) — same slope and same y-intercept → every point works
Algebraic signals — what algebra tells you
When you solve algebraically (substitution or elimination) and variables cancel out:

False statement e.g. 0 = 5 → NO solution (parallel lines — never cross)

True statement e.g. 0 = 0 → INFINITE solutions (same line — always cross)

Worked example — solve by graphing

Graphing y = 2x − 1 and y = −x + 5 → intersection at (2, 3)
The two lines intersect at (2, 3) — this is the solution to the system.
Solve: y = 2x − 1 and y = −x + 5
Step 1 — Identify slope & y-intercept for each line:   Line 1: y = 2x − 1 → m = 2, b = −1 → plot (0,−1), go up 2 right 1   Line 2: y = −x + 5 → m = −1, b = 5 → plot (0,5), go down 1 right 1 Step 2 — Find intersection:   Lines cross at (2, 3) (read from graph) Step 3 — Check in BOTH equations:   Eq 1: 3 = 2(2)−1 = 3 ✓    Eq 2: 3 = −2+5 = 3 ✓ Solution: (2, 3)
Graph: two lines intersecting at the solution
Note
Graphing gives approximate answers. Substitution and elimination give exact answers every time.

title: Solving Systems by Substitution
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: Substitution is about replacing one variable with an equivalent expression. The goal: get one equation with just ONE variable, solve it, then find the other.

Goal of substitution
Get one variable alone in one equation, then substitute that expression into the other equation. You're left with one equation and one variable — solve it!

Process for solving by substitution

  1. Solve one equation for x or y (pick whichever is easiest)
  2. Substitute that expression into the OTHER equation
  3. Solve for the remaining variable
  4. Back-substitute to find the other variable
  5. Write answer as (x, y)
  6. Check both equations
Key tip
You can solve for either variable in either equation — pick whichever is easiest (already isolated, or coefficient of 1).

Worked example 1

Solve: y = 2x − 1 and x + y = 8
Step 1 — y is already alone: y = 2x − 1 Step 2 — Substitute into Eq 2:   x + (2x − 1) = 8 ← replace y with (2x−1)   3x − 1 = 8 → 3x = 9 → x = 3 Step 3 — Back-substitute: y = 2(3) − 1 = 5 Solution: (3, 5)   Check: 5=2(3)−1 ✓ and 3+5=8 ✓

Worked example 2

Solve: 3x + y = 7 and x − 2y = 0
From Eq 2: x = 2y Substitute into Eq 1: 3(2y) + y = 7                    6y + y = 7                        7y = 7 → y = 1 Back-sub: x = 2(1) = 2 Answer: (2, 1)

title: Solving Systems by Elimination
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: Elimination is a power move — we add the two equations together to make one variable disappear. No substitution needed, just addition!

Goal of elimination
Add the two equations together to cancel (eliminate) one variable. The coefficients of that variable must be opposites (like +3y and −3y).
When to use each method
Graphing Best for visualizing; approximate answers

Substitution Best when one variable is already isolated (y=... or x=...)

Elimination Best when both equations are in standard form (ax+by=c)

Process for solving by elimination

  1. Line up the equations with like terms in columns
  2. Multiply one or both equations so that coefficients of one variable are opposites
  3. Add the equations together — one variable cancels
  4. Solve for the remaining variable
  5. Substitute back to find the other variable
  6. Check both equations
Tip
Pick the variable with the smaller coefficient to multiply — easier numbers to work with!

Worked example 1 (already set up)

Solve: 2x + 3y = 12 and −2x + y = 4
 2x + 3y = 12 +(−2x + y =  4)        4y = 16 → y = 4 Substitute y=4 into Eq 1: 2x + 12 = 12 → x = 0 Answer: (0, 4)

Worked example 2 (need to multiply first)

Solve: 3x + 2y = 8 and x − y = 1
Multiply Eq 2 by 2: 2x − 2y = 2  3x + 2y = 8 +(2x − 2y = 2)  5x       = 10 → x = 2 Substitute x=2 into Eq 2: 2 − y = 1 → y = 1 Answer: (2, 1)
Mr. Behling says: Don't let it freak you out — it's just two equations working together. Pick the method that looks easiest for the problem in front of you.

title: Translating Words to Algebra
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: Algebra is just a language. Before you can solve a word problem, you must translate the English into math. Certain key words always map to the same operations.

Key Words → Operations
Sum, plus, more than, increased by, added to:  +
Difference, less than, decreased by, subtracted from:  −
Product, times, twice (2×), double:  ×
Quotient, divided by, ratio of:  ÷
Is, equals, gives, results in:  =
A number, some number, an unknown:  x (or any variable)
Watch out: "less than" reverses order!
"5 less than a number" means x − 5, NOT 5 − x. The phrase names what comes first in the subtraction.
4-Step Problem-Solving Process
Step 1 — Define variable: Let x = ...
Step 2 — Write equation from the words
Step 3 — Solve the equation
Step 4 — Answer the question in context (with units!)

Worked example — "The difference of five times a number and two is 13. Find the number."

Worked example (from Semester 1 Final)
Let x = the number 5x − 2 = 13 5x = 15 x = 3 ✓
Joke: Why was the math book sad? Because it had too many problems.

title: One-Variable Word Problems
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: Now you apply the 4-step process to number problems, age problems, and consecutive integer problems. Always define your variable first!

Types of problems in 10.2
Number problems: "Two more than three times a number is 11."
Age problems: "In 5 years, Maria will be twice as old as Tom."
Consecutive integers: n, n+1, n+2 (consecutive) or n, n+2, n+4 (consecutive odd/even)

Worked example — consecutive integers

Worked example
Find 3 consecutive integers that sum to 48. Let n = first integer n + (n+1) + (n+2) = 48 3n + 3 = 48 3n = 45 n = 15 → integers: 15, 16, 17 ✓

Worked example — from Semester 1 Final

Worked example (Gary's Garage)
Total cost $1060. Labor $140/hr. Parts $500. Let x = number of hours 140x + 500 = 1060 140x = 560 x = 4 hours ✓

title: Geometry Word Problems
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: You know how to solve equations. Geometry word problems give you a formula (perimeter, angle sum) and a relationship between the unknown sides or angles. Set up an equation and solve.

Perimeter & Angle Sum Formulas
Rectangle: P = 2l + 2w
Triangle: P = a + b + c   and   angle sum = 180°
Quadrilateral: angle sum = 360°

Strategy: write the missing side or angle in terms of x, then plug into the formula.

Worked example — rectangle perimeter

Worked example
A rectangle's length is 3 more than its width. Perimeter = 26. Let w = width, so l = w + 3 2(w + 3) + 2w = 26 2w + 6 + 2w = 26 4w = 20 w = 5, l = 8 ✓

Worked example — triangle angles

Worked example
Triangle angles: x, 2x, and 3x. Find each angle. x + 2x + 3x = 180 6x = 180 x = 30 → angles: 30°, 60°, 90° ✓
Joke: Parallel lines have so much in common. It's a shame they'll never meet.

title: Linear Rate Problems (b + mx = y)
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: Many real-world situations have a fixed starting amount b plus a constant rate m per unit. Write: y = b + mx. Identify b and m from context, then use the equation.

b + mx = y setup
b = fixed fee (flat starting cost — even before any units)
m = rate per unit (cost per hour, per mile, per item …)
x = quantity (hours, miles, items …)
y = total

Worked example — plumber bill

Worked example
A plumber charges $75 flat plus $50 per hour. Write an equation for total cost y after x hours. y = 75 + 50x For 4 hours: y = 75 + 50(4) = $275 If bill = $325: 75 + 50x = 325 → 50x = 250 → x = 5 hrs ✓

Worked example — comparing two plans

Worked example
Plan A: $20 flat + $5/month. Plan B: $0 flat + $8/month. After how many months do they cost the same? 20 + 5x = 8x 20 = 3x x = 20/3 ≈ 6.7 months. After 7 months Plan A is cheaper. ✓
Reading hint
Look for phrases like “flat fee,” “initial charge,” or “per [unit].” The per-unit number is always m. The up-front cost is always b.

title: Two-Variable Word Problems
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: When a problem has two unknowns, you need two equations. Use the context to write a system, then solve by substitution or addition.

Setting Up a System
Step 1: Define both variables clearly (Let x = …, Let y = …)
Step 2: Find two different facts in the problem
Step 3: Write one equation from each fact
Step 4: Solve the system (substitution or elimination)
Step 5: Answer both unknowns in context with units

Worked example — tickets at a game

Worked example
Adult tickets $10, student tickets $6. Sold 200 total for $1600. Let a = adult tickets, s = student tickets Eq 1 (count): a + s = 200 Eq 2 (money): 10a + 6s = 1600 Substitute: a = 200 − s → 10(200−s) + 6s = 1600 2000 − 10s + 6s = 1600 → −4s = −400 → s = 100 a = 100, s = 100 ✓
Mr. Behling says: Two unknowns? No problem. Two equations — two facts. That's the move.

title: Rate, Time & Distance Problems
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: These problems involve movement. The key formula connects distance, rate (speed), and time.

The d = r × t Formula
d = r × t   distance = rate × time

Rearranged:   r = d/t    t = d/r
Three Situations
Same direction: difference in distances
Opposite directions: distances add up to total
Toward each other: distances add up; sum = total distance

Worked example — opposite directions

Worked example
Two cars leave at same time in opposite directions. Car A: 60 mph. Car B: 45 mph. After how many hours are they 315 miles apart? Let t = time 60t + 45t = 315 105t = 315 t = 3 hours ✓

Worked example — one object

Worked example
A train travels 240 miles in 4 hours. What is its speed? r = d/t = 240/4 = 60 mph ✓

title: Mixture & Multi-Step Problems
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: Mixture problems combine two things (quantities, concentrations, prices) to find an unknown. They use the idea of weighted averages.

System approach for mixture problems
Let x = quantity of item A
Then total − x = quantity of item B
Set up: (value of A) + (value of B) = (total value)

Worked example — from Semester 1 Final (shopping problem)

Worked example
Jeans cost $42 each. Shirts cost $12 each. Bought 5 items. Spent $126. Let j = jeans. Then 5 − j = shirts. 42j + 12(5 − j) = 126 42j + 60 − 12j = 126 30j = 66 j = 2.2... → j = 2 jeans, 3 shirts ✓
Multi-Step Strategy
Break the problem into parts. Identify what is unknown, what relationships exist, and what equation captures those relationships. Don't rush — read twice.
Joke: I told an algebra joke. No response. I guess x didn't care.

title: Zero & Negative Exponents
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: You already know that 23 = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. That's repeated multiplication. Now we extend this idea to zero exponents and negative exponents.

Base, Exponent, Power
In the expression bn:
• b is the base — the number being multiplied
• n is the exponent — how many times to multiply
• The whole thing (bn) is a power

Example: 53 = 5 × 5 × 5 = 125  (base=5, exponent=3, power=125)
Zero Exponent Rule
Anything raised to the zero power equals 1.
b0 = 1  (for any b ≠ 0)

Examples: 50 = 1  •  x0 = 1  •  (−3)0 = 1  •  1000 = 1
Watch the parentheses!
(−3)0 = 1  ← the negative is inside, so the whole thing is raised to 0.
−30 = −(30) = −1  ← only 3 is raised to 0, then we negate.

Parentheses matter!
Negative Exponent Rule
A negative exponent means reciprocal (flip it):
a−n = 1an

• Negative exponent on top of a fraction: move it to the bottom, make the exponent positive.
• Negative exponent on bottom of a fraction: move it to the top, make the exponent positive.

Examples:
x−3 = 1x3
1x−4 = x4
2−3 = 123 = 18

Worked examples

Example 1 — Simplify: 4−2
4−2 = 14² = 116
Example 2 — Simplify: x−1 · y²
x−1 = 1x = y²x
Example 3 — Simplify: 3 / x−2
x−2 is on the bottom with a negative exponent Move x² to the top (exponent becomes positive) = 3x²
Joke: Mr. Behling: “I love all of algebra, but I have to be honest. Exponents are number 40 in my heart.” (40 = 1, so they're #1!)

title: Multiplying & Dividing Powers
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: When you multiply or divide two powers with the same base, there are shortcuts so you don't have to expand everything.

Prerequisite reminder — base and exponent
In bn: the base (b) is the number being multiplied, and the exponent (n) is how many times.

x3 = x × x × x  (three factors)   •   x5 = x × x × x × x × x  (five factors)

This “expanded” view is exactly why the shortcuts below work.
Multiplying Powers — Same Base
am × an = am+n
When multiplying powers with the same base, ADD the exponents.

Why? x3 · x5 = (x·x·x)(x·x·x·x·x) = x8  ✓
Dividing Powers — Same Base
aman = am−n
When dividing powers with the same base, SUBTRACT the exponents.

Top-heavy-bottom-heavy approach: bring the larger exponent to its side and subtract.

Example: x7x3 = x7−3 = x4
Coefficients are separate!
Handle coefficients (numbers out front) separately from the variable exponents.
(2x3)(5x2) = (2×5)(x3+2) = 10x5

Worked examples

Multiply: x3 · x5
Same base (x) → ADD exponents = x3+5 = x8
Multiply: (2x3)(5x²)
Coefficients: 2 × 5 = 10 Variables: x³ · x² = x3+2 = x5 = 10x5
Multiply: (4x²)(3x4)
Coefficients: 4 × 3 = 12 Variables: x² · x⁴ = x2+4 = x6 = 12x6
Divide: x9x3
Same base (x) → SUBTRACT exponents = x9−3 = x6
Divide: 12x74x2
Coefficients: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 Variables: x7−2 = x5 = 3x5
Divide: x5x8
5 − 8 = −3 = x−3 = 1x³ (apply negative exponent rule)
Exponent Expansion: x³ · x² = x⁵

title: Raising a Power to a Power
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: Now we look at what happens when an entire power is raised to another power — like (x3)4.

Power to a Power Rule
(am)n = am × n
When a power is raised to a power, MULTIPLY the exponents.

Why? (x3)4 means x3 multiplied 4 times = x3+3+3+3 = x12  ✓
Distribute to ALL factors!
When you raise a product inside parentheses to a power, the outer exponent applies to every factor inside — coefficient AND variable(s).

(2x²)³ = 2³ · (x²)³ = 8x6  ← don't forget to cube the 2!

Worked examples

Example 1 — (x²)5
Multiply the exponents: 2 × 5 = 10 = x10
Example 2 — (3x4)²
Apply exponent to each factor: 3² = 9   and   (x4)² = x4×2 = x8 = 9x8
Example 3 — (2x³y)³
Apply exponent to each factor: 2³ = 8   and   (x³)³ = x9   and   y³ = y³ = 8x9y³

title: Exponential Functions (Part 1)
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: You know linear patterns — add or subtract the same amount each time. Exponential patterns are different: you multiply or divide by the same number (the common ratio) each time.

Two types of patterns
Linear: Add or subtract a constant each step (y goes up/down by the same amount)
  Example: 2, 5, 8, 11, 14 → +3 each time

Exponential: Multiply or divide by a constant each step (y grows/shrinks by a factor)
  Example: 2, 6, 18, 54 → ×3 each time
Standard form of an exponential function
y = abx

a = y-intercept (the starting value, where x = 0)
b = the common ratio (multiplier)
  • If b > 1 → GROWTH (curve goes up)
  • If 0 < b < 1 → DECAY (curve goes down toward zero)

Key attributes

Growth vs. Decay
Both have y-intercept at a. Growth curves rise; decay curves fall toward the x-axis.
Domain, Range, and y-intercept
y-intercept: at x = 0, y = a (plug in zero for x: b0 = 1, so y = a)
Domain: all real numbers
Range: y > 0 (for positive a; the curve never touches the x-axis)

Average Rate of Change

Formula
Average Rate of Change = (f(x₂) − f(x₁)) / (x₂ − x₁)
This is “rise over run” for curves — unlike lines, it changes at every interval!

Worked example — y = 2(3x)

Evaluate y = 2(3x) for x = 0, 1, 2, 3
x = 0: y = 2(3&sup0;) = 2(1) = 2 x = 1: y = 2(3¹) = 2(3) = 6 x = 2: y = 2(3²) = 2(9) = 18 x = 3: y = 2(3³) = 2(27) = 54 b = 3 > 1 → GROWTH. y-intercept = 2. Domain: all reals. Range: y > 0.
Joke: The population of Ireland is exponential. Every year it's Dublin. (Doubling.)

title: Exponential Functions (Part 2)
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: In 12.1 you evaluated functions. Now we work backwards — given a graph or table, determine the equation y = abx. Mr. Behling loves “backwards” problems!

How to find the equation from a table or graph
Step 1 — Find a: Read the y-intercept (where x = 0). That is your “a” value.
Step 2 — Find b: Divide any y-value by the previous y-value (consecutive values). That is your common ratio “b”.
Step 3 — Write it: y = abx
Growth or decay? If b > 1 → growth; if 0 < b < 1 → decay.

Worked example 1 — from a table

Table: x = 0, 1, 2, 3 and y = 5, 10, 20, 40
Step 1: x=0 gives y=5 → a = 5 Step 2: ratio = 10/5 = 2 → b = 2 Equation: y = 5(2x) — GROWTH (b=2>1)

Worked example 2 — from a graph

Graph shows y-intercept at 8 and the curve is decreasing, halving each time
a = 8 (y-intercept from graph) b = 1/2 (halving each step) Equation: y = 8(1/2)x — DECAY (0 < b < 1)
Graph: y = 8(1/2)x — decay curve with y-intercept and asymptote

title: Exponential Function Word Problems
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: Real-world situations often follow exponential patterns. You can now write and evaluate exponential growth and exponential decay models from word problems.

Formulas
Growth: A = A₀(1 + r)t
Decay: A = A₀(1 − r)t

A₀ = initial amount, r = rate (as a decimal), t = time
Real-world examples
Growth: Population, bacteria, investments, COVID spread
Decay: Radioactive decay, car depreciation, cooling

Worked example 1 — population growth

100 frogs, 22% annual growth — after 5 years
A = 100(1 + 0.22)5 = 100(1.22)5 = 100(2.703) ≈ 270 frogs

Worked example 2 — population decline

1200 birds, 5% decline, 2019–2029 (10 years)
A = 1200(1 − 0.05)10 = 1200(0.95)10 = 1200(0.5987) ≈ 718 birds

Worked example 3 — depreciation

Car worth $30,000 in 2026, depreciates 15%/year — value in 2030 (4 years later)
A = 30000(1 − 0.15)4 = 30000(0.85)4 = 30000(0.5220) ≈ $15,660
Joke: How do you know your dentist was good at algebra? She tells you that more candy leads to exponential decay.

title: Solving Exponential Equations
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: When two exponential expressions are equal AND have the same base, their exponents must be equal. This is the key rule for solving exponential equations.

Key concept
If bm = bn, then m = n. (Same base, equal → exponents are equal.)

Method 1 (same base already): Set exponents equal, solve.
Method 2 (convert to same base): Rewrite using powers (e.g., 4 = 2², 8 = 2³, 9 = 3², 27 = 3³).
Method 3 (can't match bases): Use a graphing calculator — graph both sides, find intersection.
Powers to know cold
Powers of 2: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256
Powers of 3: 3, 9, 27, 81
Powers of 4: 4, 16, 64
Powers of 5: 5, 25, 125

Worked examples

Example 1: Solve 2x = 16
2x = 16 = 24 Same base! Set exponents equal: x = 4
Example 2: Solve 3x = 27
3x = 27 = 33 Same base! x = 3
Example 3: Solve 4x = 8 (different bases → convert to base 2)
4x = 8 → (22)x = 23 2(2x) = 23 Same base! 2x = 3 → x = 3/2

title: Introduction to Polynomials
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: You've been working with expressions that have variables. A polynomial is just a collection of terms with non-negative integer exponents — no square roots, no negative exponents, no variables in denominators.

Types of Polynomials
Monomial: 1 term   (e.g., 5x²)
Binomial: 2 terms   (e.g., 3x + 4)
Trinomial: 3 terms   (e.g., x² + 2x − 5)

Degree: The highest exponent in the polynomial
Standard form: Write terms in descending order of degree
Leading coefficient: Coefficient of the highest-degree term

Worked example — identify degree and leading coefficient

Worked example
Polynomial: 4x³ − 7x + 2 Degree: 3 (highest exponent is 3) Leading coefficient: 4 Standard form: already in order ✓

Worked example — write in standard form

Worked example
5 + 3x² − x → 3x² − x + 5 (descending order: degree 2, then 1, then 0)
Joke: Why can't you trust a polynomial? Because they always have terms.

title: Adding & Subtracting Polynomials
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: Adding and subtracting polynomials is really just combining like terms. Remember: like terms have the same variable AND the same exponent.

Adding Polynomials
Identify like terms and combine. Like terms: same variable, same exponent.
x² and 3x² are like terms.   x² and x³ are NOT.
Subtracting Polynomials — DANGER ZONE
When subtracting, distribute the negative sign to EVERY term in the second polynomial. Use parentheses! Say it out loud as you go.

Worked example — adding

Worked example
(3x² + 2x − 1) + (x² − 5x + 4) = (3x² + x²) + (2x − 5x) + (−1 + 4) = 4x² − 3x + 3 ✓

Worked example — subtracting

Worked example — distribute the negative!
(5x² + 3x − 2) − (2x² − x + 1) = 5x² + 3x − 2 − 2x² + x − 1 ← distribute − = 3x² + 4x − 3 ✓

title: Multiplying Polynomials (Monomial × Polynomial)
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: Use the distributive property to multiply a monomial by every term in the polynomial. When multiplying variables, add exponents (from Unit 11).

Rules for Monomial Multiplication
Coefficients: multiply together
Same-base variables: add the exponents
Example: 3x² × 4x³ = 12x⁵

Worked example — distribute

Worked example
3x(2x² − 5x + 4) = 3x(2x²) + 3x(−5x) + 3x(4) = 6x³ − 15x² + 12x ✓
Worked example 2
−2x²(3x − 7) = −2x²(3x) + (−2x²)(−7) = −6x³ + 14x² ✓
Distribution: 3x × (2x² − 5x + 4)

title: Multiplying Polynomials (Binomial × Binomial — FOIL)
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: When multiplying two binomials, use FOIL to make sure you multiply every term by every other term.

FOIL = First + Outer + Inner + Last
(a + b)(c + d):
First: a × c
Outer: a × d
Inner: b × c
Last: b × d
Then combine like terms.
Same method, different name
Some textbooks and teachers call this the “Clamshell Method” because the curved arcs connecting each pair of terms look like a clamshell when drawn. If you encounter that name, it is exactly the same process as FOIL — just a different nickname for the same moves.

Worked example — (x + 3)(x + 5)

Worked example
F: x × x = x² O: x × 5 = 5x I: 3 × x = 3x L: 3 × 5 = 15 = x² + 5x + 3x + 15 = x² + 8x + 15 ✓

Worked example — (2x − 3)(x + 4)

Worked example
F: 2x × x = 2x² O: 2x × 4 = 8x I: −3 × x = −3x L: −3 × 4 = −12 = 2x² + 8x − 3x − 12 = 2x² + 5x − 12 ✓
Special Case: Difference of Squares
(a + b)(a − b) = a² − b²
Example: (x + 4)(x − 4) = x² − 16
FOIL Box: (x + 3)(x + 5)
Joke: What did the polynomial say to the monomial? You're just a part of a bigger picture.

title: Introduction to Factoring
html:
Big picture: Quadratic equations (degree-2 polynomials) need new solving techniques. Factoring is the first one. Think of it as distribution in reverse — multiplication backwards. To factor confidently, you need to know your multiplication facts.

Key concept — what is factoring?
Factoring = breaking a polynomial into the product of its factors
= distribution in reverse

Distribution: 3x(2x + 3) = 6x² + 9x
Factoring: 6x² + 9x = 3x(2x + 3) ← same thing, backwards

Greatest Common Factor (GCF)

GCF = Greatest Common Factor
The largest factor that appears in ALL terms of the expression.

Always check for GCF first before any other factoring technique. Always.
How to factor out the GCF
Step 1 — Find the GCF of all coefficients and all variable parts
Step 2 — Write the GCF outside parentheses
Step 3 — Divide each term by the GCF and write inside parentheses
Step 4 — Check by distributing back

Worked examples

Example 1 — Factor: 6x² + 9x
GCF of 6 and 9 = 3. GCF of x² and x = x. GCF = 3x 6x² + 9x = 3x(2x + 3) ← divide each term by 3x Check: 3x · 2x + 3x · 3 = 6x² + 9x ✓
Example 2 — Factor: 12x³ − 8x² + 4x
GCF of 12, 8, 4 = 4. GCF of x³, x², x = x. GCF = 4x 12x³ − 8x² + 4x = 4x(3x² − 2x + 1) Check by distributing ✓
Example 3 — Factor: 15x²y − 10xy²
GCF of 15 and 10 = 5. GCF of variables = xy. 15x²y − 10xy² = 5xy(3x − 2y)
Joke: Did you hear that old math teachers never die? They just lose some of their functions.

title: Factoring Trinomials (Part 1)
html:
When to use this: When the leading coefficient is 1 (i.e., the trinomial looks like x² + bx + c). Very first step: always factor out the GCF first, even if the GCF is 1.

The shortcut — find two numbers
For x² + bx + c: find two numbers p and q such that
   p × q = c (they multiply to the constant)
   p + q = b (they add to the middle coefficient)

Then: x² + bx + c = (x + p)(x + q)
The X Method
Draw an X. Write the product (c) on TOP. Write the sum (b) on the BOTTOM.
Fill in the two sides = two numbers that multiply to the top and add to the bottom.

Worked examples

Example 1 — Factor: x² + 7x + 12
Step 1: GCF = 1 (nothing to factor out) Step 2: Find p and q: p × q = 12, p + q = 7 Try: 3 × 4 = 12, 3 + 4 = 7 ✓ Answer: (x + 3)(x + 4) Check by FOIL: x² + 4x + 3x + 12 = x² + 7x + 12 ✓
Example 2 — Factor: x² + 2x − 15
p × q = −15, p + q = 2 Try: 5 × (−3) = −15, 5 + (−3) = 2 ✓ Answer: (x + 5)(x − 3)
Example 3 — Factor: x² − 9x + 20
p × q = 20, p + q = −9 Try: (−4) × (−5) = 20, (−4) + (−5) = −9 ✓ Answer: (x − 4)(x − 5)
Reverse Box: x² + 7x + 12

title: Factoring Trinomials (Part 2)
html:
Now we handle cases where the shortcut from 14.2 doesn’t apply: a ≠ 1, negative leading term, and the special Difference of Squares pattern.

When the first term is negative
Factor out −1 first! This changes all signs inside and makes the leading coefficient positive, so you can use normal methods.
Split the Middle Term method (a ≠ 1)
For ax² + bx + c where a ≠ 1:
Step 1 — Multiply a · c (call it k)
Step 2 — Find two numbers that × = k and + = b
Step 3 — Split the middle term into two terms using those numbers
Step 4 — Factor by grouping: group first two terms, group last two terms, factor each group, factor out common binomial
Difference of Squares
a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b)

Recognize it: two perfect squares with a subtraction sign between them.
Examples: x² − 25 = (x + 5)(x − 5)    4x² − 9 = (2x + 3)(2x − 3)

Worked examples

Example 1 — Factor: 2x² + 7x + 3 (a = 2)
a · c = 2 × 3 = 6 Find: p × q = 6, p + q = 7 → 1 and 6 Split: 2x² + 1x + 6x + 3 ← split 7x into 1x + 6x Group: x(2x + 1) + 3(2x + 1) Factor binomial: (x + 3)(2x + 1)
Example 2 — Factor: −x² + 5x − 6
First term is negative → factor out −1 −1(x² − 5x + 6) Now factor inside: p × q = 6, p + q = −5 → (−2) and (−3) Answer: −(x − 2)(x − 3)
Example 3 — Factor: 9x² − 16
Recognize Difference of Squares: (3x)² − 4² Answer: (3x + 4)(3x − 4)
Box Model: 2x² + 7x + 3 (a ≠ 1)

title: Solving Equations by Factoring
html:
Big idea: Now that we can factor, we can use the Zero Product Property to solve quadratic equations.

Zero Product Property (ZPP)
If A · B = 0, then A = 0 OR B = 0

Think about it: the only way a product equals zero is if at least one factor is zero.
Process: Solving equations by factoring (5 steps)
Step 1 — Move all terms to one side = 0
Step 2 — Factor completely (GCF first!)
Step 3 — Apply Zero Product Property: set each factor = 0
Step 4 — Solve each linear equation
Step 5 — Check solutions in the original equation

Worked examples

Example 1 — Solve: x² + 5x + 6 = 0
Already = 0. Factor: (x + 2)(x + 3) = 0 ZPP: x + 2 = 0  OR  x + 3 = 0 x = −2  OR  x = −3
Example 2 — Solve: x² − 7x = 0
Factor out GCF: x(x − 7) = 0 ZPP: x = 0  OR  x − 7 = 0 x = 0  OR  x = 7
Example 3 — Solve: 2x² + x = 1
Move everything to one side: 2x² + x − 1 = 0 Factor: (2x − 1)(x + 1) = 0 ZPP: 2x − 1 = 0  OR  x + 1 = 0 x = 1/2  OR  x = −1
Always check!
Plug both answers back into the original equation to verify.

title: Introduction to Quadratic Functions
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: Linear functions make straight lines. Quadratic functions make U-shaped curves called parabolas. The parent function is y = x².

Standard Form of a Quadratic
y = ax² + bx + c

a > 0: parabola opens UP (makes a U)
a < 0: parabola opens DOWN (makes an upside-down U)
|a| > 1: narrower than parent
|a| < 1: wider than parent
y-intercept: always the value of c (set x = 0)
Parent Function: y = x²
x −3 −2 −1 0 1 2 3
y 9 4 1 0 1 4 9
Notice: symmetric around x = 0 (the axis of symmetry). The vertex is at (0, 0).
Direction of Opening
Worked example — identify attributes of y = 2x² − 3x + 5
Identify a, b, c: a = 2, b = −3, c = 5 Direction: a = 2 > 0 → opens UP (minimum vertex) Width: |a| = 2 > 1 → narrower than parent y = x² y-intercept: set x = 0 → y = 5 → point (0, 5)
Axis of symmetry — preview
Every parabola has a vertical axis of symmetry that divides it into two mirror halves. It passes through the vertex.

Formula: x = −b ÷ (2a)

Example: y = 2x² − 3x + 5  (a=2, b=−3)  →  x = −(−3) ÷ (2×2) = 3⁄4

You will apply this formula in depth starting in Topic 15.2.
Domain and range of a parabola
Domain: always all real numbers — any x value is allowed.

Range: depends on vertex and direction of opening:
• Opens UP (a > 0): range is y ≥ k (vertex y-value)  ← the vertex is the minimum
• Opens DOWN (a < 0): range is y ≤ k (vertex y-value)  ← the vertex is the maximum
Joke: Why was the math book sad? Because it had too many problems.

title: Vertex & Axis of Symmetry
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: Every parabola has a vertex (the highest or lowest point) and a axis of symmetry (a vertical line through the vertex).

Finding Axis of Symmetry and Vertex
Axis of symmetry: x = −b2a
Vertex: plug AOS x-value back into the equation to find y

If a > 0: vertex is the minimum
If a < 0: vertex is the maximum

Worked example — y = x² + 4x + 3

Worked example
a = 1, b = 4, c = 3 AOS: x = −42×1 = −42 = −2 Vertex y: y = (−2)² + 4(−2) + 3 = 4 − 8 + 3 = −1 Vertex: (−2, −1). Minimum (a > 0) ✓
Parabola with Vertex and Axis of Symmetry

title: Graphing in Standard Form
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: To graph a quadratic from standard form, you follow a systematic 5-step process. Use Desmos to check your work!

5-Step Graphing Process (Standard Form)
Step 1: Find axis of symmetry: x = −b2a
Step 2: Find vertex (plug AOS into equation)
Step 3: Find y-intercept (set x = 0 → y = c)
Step 4: Find symmetric points (reflect y-intercept)
Step 5: Draw smooth parabola through all points

Worked example — y = x² − 6x + 8

Worked example — all 5 steps
a=1, b=−6, c=8 Step 1 — AOS: x = −b2a = −(−6)/(2×1) = 6/2 = 3 Step 2 — Vertex: y = 3²−6(3)+8 = 9−18+8 = −1 → vertex: (3, −1) ← minimum Step 3 — y-intercept: x=0 → y=8 → point (0, 8) Step 4 — Symmetric point: (0,8) is 3 units left of AOS → mirror: (6, 8) Step 5: Draw upward parabola through (0,8), (2,0), (3,−1), (4,0), (6,8) ✓
Key Points for y = x²−6x+8
x y = x²−6x+8 Point
0 8 (0, 8) ← y-int
2 0 (2, 0) ← x-int
3 −1 (3, −1) ← vertex
4 0 (4, 0) ← x-int
6 8 (6, 8) ← symmetric to (0,8)
Graph: y = x²−6x+8 (plot the 5 key points)

title: Graphing in Vertex Form
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: Vertex form makes graphing even easier because the vertex is visible right in the equation.

Vertex Form
y = a(x − h)² + k

Vertex: (h, k) — read directly from equation
h: horizontal shift (opposite sign from what you see!)
k: vertical shift
a: determines direction and width (same as standard form)
Step-by-step from vertex form
Step 1: Read (h, k) directly from y = a(x − h)² + k → that's your vertex
Step 2: Check a: positive = opens up, negative = opens down
Step 3: Plot the vertex (h, k)
Step 4: Go 1 unit left and right from the vertex; go up (or down) |a| units
Step 5: Draw the smooth parabola through all three points
Watch the sign of h!
y = (x − 3)² + 1 → vertex is (3, 1) NOT (−3, 1). The h value is whatever makes (x − h) = 0.

Worked example — y = 2(x − 3)² + 1

Worked example
a = 2, h = 3, k = 1 Vertex: (3, 1). Opens up. Narrow (a=2). Graph: start at (3,1). Go right 1 → up 2: (4, 3). Go left 1 → up 2: (2, 3).

Worked example — y = −(x + 2)² + 4

Worked example — y = −(x+2)² + 4
Rewrite: y = −1(x − (−2))² + 4 Step 1 — Read vertex: h = −2, k = 4 → Vertex: (−2, 4) Step 2 — Direction: a = −1 < 0 → opens DOWN (maximum) Step 3 — Points: 1 right → (−1, 3); 1 left → (−3, 3) Step 4 — Draw downward parabola through (−3,3), (−2,4), (−1,3) ✓
Graph: y = −(x+2)² + 4 (vertex form, opens down)
Joke: I told an algebra joke. No response. I guess x didn't care.

title: Quadratic Word Problems
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: You already know how to find the vertex, x-intercepts, and y-intercept of a parabola. In word problems, those features have real-world meaning. The vertex is the maximum or minimum value. The x-intercepts are the zeros (where the value is 0). The y-intercept is the starting value.

Projectile Motion Setup
h(t) = −16t² + v₀t + h₀  (feet)

• t = time in seconds
• h(t) = height at time t
• v₀ = initial velocity (ft/s)
• h₀ = initial height (y-intercept = starting height)
• Vertex = maximum height and the time when it occurs
• x-intercepts (zeros) = when the object hits the ground (h = 0)
Reading the graph
y-intercept → starting height. Vertex → max height (read both coordinates: time and height). x-intercept (positive one) → when it lands. Width of parabola above x-axis → total time in the air.
Projectile: h(t) = −16t² + 64t (launched from ground)

Worked example — ball launched upward

h(t) = −16t² + 48t + 0
Starting height (y-intercept): h(0) = 0  → starts at ground level Time at max height (AOS): t = −48 ÷ (2 × −16) = −48 ÷ (−32) = 1.5 s Max height (vertex y-value): h(1.5) = −16(2.25) + 48(1.5) = −36 + 72 = 36 ft Lands when h = 0: 0 = −16t² + 48t = t(−16t + 48) → t = 0 or t = 3  → lands at t = 3 s

Worked example — factored form context

A ball follows h(t) = −(t − 1)(t − 5) — find max height
Zeros: t = 1 and t = 5 (the ball is at h=0 at these times) AOS (midpoint of zeros): t = (1 + 5) ÷ 2 = 3 Max height: h(3) = −(3 − 1)(3 − 5) = −(2)(−2) = 4 Answer: max height = 4 units at t = 3 s ✓
Mr. Behling says: The ball always comes back down. So does the grade — unless you study the vertex!

title: Solving by Square Roots
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: When a quadratic has no x term (just x² and a constant), you can solve it directly by taking square roots. Remember: every positive number has TWO square roots!

Square Root Method
Works when: no x term (b = 0 in ax² + bx + c = 0)

Steps: (1) Get x² alone   (2) Take ±√ of both sides   (3) Simplify

Always write ± — there are two solutions unless the right side is 0!
Three Possible Cases

Worked examples

Example 1 — x² = 25
x = ±√25 = ±5 x = 5   or   x = −5 ✓
Example 2 — 3x² − 12 = 0
3x² = 12 x² = 4 x = ±2 ✓
Example 3 — x² + 16 = 0
x² = −16 → no real solution (√ of negative)
Joke: Why did the quadratic equation feel so lonely? Because it didn't know where its roots were.

title: Solving by Factoring
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: In Unit 14 you learned to factor polynomials. Now you use factoring to solve equations by applying the Zero Product Property. The key insight: if two things multiply to zero, at least one of them must be zero.

Zero Product Property (ZPP)
If A × B = 0, then A = 0 OR B = 0

Process for solving by factoring (5 steps):
1. Write in standard form: ax2 + bx + c = 0
2. Find the factor pair: two numbers that × = c and + = b
3. Write the factored form: (x + p)(x + q) = 0
4. Apply ZPP: set each factor = 0
5. Solve each resulting linear equation — then check!

Worked example 1 — x2 + 5x + 6 = 0

All 5 steps — trinomial, a = 1
Step 1 — Standard form:   x2 + 5x + 6 = 0  a = 1, b = 5, c = 6. Already in standard form. Step 2 — Find factor pair (× = c, + = b):   Need two numbers that × = 6 and + = 5   Try 1 × 6 = 6 → 1 + 6 = 7 ✗  |  Try 2 × 3 = 6 → 2 + 3 = 5 ✓ Step 3 — Factored form:   (x + 2)(x + 3) = 0 Step 4 — Apply ZPP:   x + 2 = 0      OR      x + 3 = 0 Step 5 — Solve each factor:   x = −2              x = −3 Check: (−2)2+5(−2)+6 = 4−10+6 = 0 ✓  |  (−3)2+5(−3)+6 = 9−15+6 = 0 ✓

Worked example 2 — x2 − 7x + 12 = 0

All 5 steps — both factors negative
Step 1 — Standard form:   x2 − 7x + 12 = 0  a = 1, b = −7, c = 12 Step 2 — Find factor pair (× = 12, + = −7):   Try −3 × −4 = 12 → −3 + (−4) = −7 ✓ Step 3 — Factored form:   (x − 3)(x − 4) = 0 Step 4 — Apply ZPP:   x − 3 = 0      OR      x − 4 = 0 Step 5 — Solve:   x = 3                   x = 4 Check: 32−7(3)+12 = 9−21+12 = 0 ✓  |  42−7(4)+12 = 16−28+12 = 0 ✓

Worked example 3 — x2 − 5x = 0 (GCF case)

All 5 steps — factor out GCF, not a trinomial
Step 1 — Standard form:   x2 − 5x = 0  c = 0, so there is no constant term Step 2 — Find factor pair:   GCF of x2 and −5x is x. Factor it out. Step 3 — Factored form:   x(x − 5) = 0 Step 4 — Apply ZPP:   x = 0        OR      x − 5 = 0 Step 5 — Solve:   x = 0                   x = 5
Don't divide both sides by x!
If you divide x2 − 5x = 0 by x, you get x − 5 = 0 and only find x = 5. You lose x = 0.
Rule: Never divide by a variable — always factor it out instead.
Roots = where the parabola crosses the x-axis (ZPP sets each factor to zero)

title: The Quadratic Formula
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: The quadratic formula works for ANY quadratic equation — even ones that can't be factored easily. It comes from completing the square on the general form.

The Quadratic Formula
For ax² + bx + c = 0:
x = −b ± √(b² − 4ac)2a

Steps: (1) Write in standard form ax²+bx+c=0   (2) Identify a, b, c   (3) Plug in   (4) Simplify both solutions

Worked example — x² − 5x + 6 = 0

Worked example
a=1, b=−5, c=6 x = 5 ± √(25 − 24)2 = 5 ± √12 = 5 ± 12 x = 5+12 = 3    or    x = 5−12 = 2 ✓

Worked example — 2x² + 3x − 2 = 0

Worked example
a=2, b=3, c=−2 x = −3 ± √(9 + 16)4 = −3 ± √254 = −3 ± 54 x = 2/4 = 1/2    or    x = −84 = −2 ✓
Joke: I tried to factor x²−4 but it fell apart into (x+2)(x−2).

title: Discriminant & Types of Solutions
html:
Connect to prior knowledge: The expression under the radical in the quadratic formula is called the discriminant. It tells you how many real solutions exist WITHOUT solving the full equation.

Discriminant = b² − 4ac
D > 0: TWO distinct real solutions (parabola crosses x-axis twice)
D = 0: ONE real solution (parabola touches x-axis at vertex)
D < 0: NO real solutions (parabola doesn't cross x-axis)

Worked examples

Example 1 — x² − 5x + 4
D = (−5)² − 4(1)(4) = 25 − 16 = 9 D = 9 > 0 → two real solutions ✓
Example 2 — x² − 4x + 4
D = 16 − 16 = 0 D = 0 → one real solution (double root) ✓
Example 3 — x² + 2x + 5
D = 4 − 20 = −16 D = −16 < 0 → no real solutions ✓
